questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Academic excellence and school reputation, beautiful and large campus, proximity to family.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: An absolutely fantastic experience that I would recommend to everyone!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy to find lots of information. The hard thing to navigate was more the overload of information (see next box).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
We were presented with emails, webpages, webinars, physical orientation etc. – all packed with information about how to navigate all aspects of Berkeley, special offers at Berkeley, advice on being at Berkeley, tips and tricks for doing well and Berkeley etc. 

I talked to other visiting students to figure out what information was essential and what information could be ignored. This definitely made it more manageable.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was in a particularly lucky situation were I already knew some people living right next to campus before I went on exchange. So it was very easy for me, as they offered me a room at their place.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Although I didn't live at I-house myself, I quickly made friends there and visited a lot. If I was going to Berkeley again, I would probably try to get a room at I-house. Sure, it is expensive – but it seems worth it with 3 meals a day (food is very expensive in Berkeley) and all the priceless social experiences and friends most people seemed to make there.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I-house seems like the perfect option. It could be cheaper however.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Berkeley has an add/drop system with course enrollment opening up asynchronously for different groups at different times. Depending on what year you are, what you are studying and what program you are on, your enrollment will be different. It is not hard to find your time slot though, as it is pretty clear on their website. However, the process is still quite stressful as one has to "snatch" a spot as if it was a festival ticket (if one is applying to popular courses). And many people will choose way too many courses in this period and then drop them within 2 weeks after school starts in which case spots slowly open up in some courses, meaning you might still get a spot. So in reality there might be a 2 month delay between initial course enrollment and when ones final course schedule is decided.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: However, I still gave the process a 2/5 (and not a 1/5) on above scale as there is great "Academic advising" at Berkeley which you can contact easily and get assistance from.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very satisfied with the courses I ended up taking, and so I would say that I was successful. However, I had my initial enrollment on July 15th and only ended up getting a spot in the graduate course I really wanted around September.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Don't despair if you don't get all your intended courses immediately. Just keep showing up to the classes and get on the waitlist as soon as possible! Then if a spot opens up and you get it, you won't be 2 weeks behind on classes. 

And if it all seems a bit overwhelming don't hesitate to ask fellow students once you arrive or contact academic advising within your department at Berkeley.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took three "Upper Division" BA courses, and one MA course. The "College of Letters & Science" only allows for exchange students to take one MA course, although I wanted to take more MA courses initially. However, the course combination I had was quite challenging for me, so I am glad I ended with only a single MA course. Although I will say that I heard at Berkeley that the Upper Division courses famously often have a higher workload (in terms of assignments and quizzes) than certain MA courses. Hence it might be very doable to do multiple MA courses. In this case, a tip is to apply through the Statistics Department (if possible), since I believe they don't limit MA courses – and regardless of department, one can enroll in basically any courses at Berkeley (I recommend "fact-checking" this by emailing the department and/or UCPH to clarify what is possible and what is not).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was actually pretty comparable. Lectures were a bit shorter (50 or 80 minutes of actual lecture time), but then there were more sessions per week). Great teachers and courses at high levels. A big difference was the concept of "Office Hours" instead of TA sessions. "Office Hours" are designated time slots set aside by the professors for students to show up and ask questions in more intimate settings. I am used to TA sessions and I know that we are always allowed to show up at our professors' offices at UCHP, but at Berkeley it was very systematic and expected to show up at their offices, which I found pretty cool!

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Upper Division BA courses: Introduction to Complex Analysis, Introduction to Partial Differential Equations and Introduction to Quantum Field Theory

MA course: Differential Topology

DeCal / Seminars (only 2 ECTS per course; these were "for fun"): Introduction to Go and Berkeley Connect.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I wholeheartedly recommend the courses I took in the Math department: Introduction to Complex Analysis, Introduction to Partial Differential Equations and Differential Topology. 

I found my Introduction to Quantum Field Theory course hard to follow along with simultaneously and so I did not get as good an impression of this course. Looking back at it now though, I am very glad that I took it. I learned more than I thought at the time, and am glad to have seen the material.

I also recommend taking a DeCal ("Democratic Education at Cal") which are these small "for fun" courses for 1 or 2 units, taught by other Berkeley Students. The Berkeley Connect course was also pretty cool, as we got to meet a Nobel Prize winner for a Q and A session and go on lab tours!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I hadn't done a big enough travel budget. Make sure to allocate money for fun experiences!

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were very expensive. So was the rent!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: UC Berkeley has an insane amount of clubs (I think more than 1000 registered!) and activities of all kinds.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Free gym with swimming pool, weight room, dance room, basketball courts, badminton courts, ping pong courts, climbing walls, squash courts etc.! Best part: You can borrow rackets and balls.

There were also often different types of events or club meet-ups at the campus.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Make sure to sign up for "Intramural Sports" (IM sports). 

Make sure to go to American Football games as often as you can (good vibes!). Also, be sure to try and attend other big sports events: Basketball games, baseball games, volleyball games, swim meets etc. It's a big part of college culture, and very fun to meet all the nice people that attend. 

Make sure to go to "Taco Tuesday" at Raleigh's Pub with friends. Even if you are not the big party-go'er, it's a lovely atmosphere and a cheap dinner. Just go at around 7 or 8 pm and enjoy the vibes! If you then like dancing, you can join the other's and go to "Tap House" when Rayleigh's close their outdoor area. 

Make sure to attend "The Big Game" if possible (student tickets are way cheaper than regular seating – and more fun!)

Check out the "Rose Gardens" and the botanic garden.

See if you can get to spend Thanksgiving with an American family (they have to invite you of course). This was an awesome experience!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to Yosemite, Lake Tahoe and a proper trip to San Francisco if it's clear so one can see the bridge.

Maybe visit Carmel-by-the-Sea or do a wine tasting in Sonoma county / Napa valley. 

Or check out guides yourself on the internet – California has amazing nature!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. People are extremely open and friendly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
As long as you have the courage to say hi and not worry about looking like a fool, then you will have the best time ever. People are so nice if you meet them with a smile!

Americans will be quite enthusiastic and optimistic – lean into it, and join them! There are lots of things to be excited about at Berkeley. 

Go to cafés with people from your classes after they end and talk about the material (or at least act like that's the plan, until you end up chatting about life instead ;) )

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: No important differences. However, I don't recommend talking politics with your friends. I avoided this on purpose for the most part, because I know that in America you will often vote on the same party and politicians as your family or childhood friends. So it was really hard for me to connect the person with the politics they supported often, because they honestly was just voting on a specific politician because they had learned to do so. Hence I don't think there's any good to come out of spending time on politics.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The openness, friendliness and level of excitement and energy I met every day. People did tons of stuff and were very larger-than-life characters, all very happy to share and ready to cheer you on!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Be courageous and approach people you don't know. Don't be afraid to look or sound awkward, but instead turn it around and make it your goal to make a little bit of a fool out of yourself every day. Then you will meet tons of great people and have fantastic laughs.
- Take classes you think sound interesting, not the ones you think will be easy. You will find way more people to connect with.
- Say YES to experiences. Plan trips. Enjoy the campus (don't forget to go up the Campanile often – it's free for students!!)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to ask your fellow students and friends for help, tips and tricks. You'll figure most of it out once you get there. And once again, it is a big recommendation to stay at the I-house.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: That I learned to believe more in myself and embrace the fun of it.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Taking multiple hard courses at once, forcing me to abandon perfectionism.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: DO IT! Go on exchange! You will learn way more than you think – both academically and personally.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
